title: Prediction of "class" and "score" seems incorrect
description:
I'll use `lda_schafer()` as an example, but other classifiers seems to have the same problem too.

For `predict.lda_schafer(model, newdata, type = "class")`, the class is predicted in line 159 of [lda-schafer.r](https://github.com/topepo/sparsediscrim/blob/main/R/lda-schafer.r#L159) by the function `score_to_class()` in [helper.r](https://github.com/topepo/sparsediscrim/blob/main/R/helper.r#L238), which will pick the class with the lowest score. The score `predict.lda_schafer(model, newdata, type = "score")` is calculated in line 146 of [lda-schafer.r](https://github.com/topepo/sparsediscrim/blob/main/R/lda-schafer.r#L146) by `with(class_est, quadform(object$cov_inv, obs - xbar) + log(prior))`, which I guess computes $(x - \mu_k)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x - \mu_k) + \log(\pi_k)$.

However, this calculation looks very strange. The larger the `prior` for a class, the more likely `x` should be in this class. But with this calculation, the `score` will become larger with larger `prior`, and according to your decision rule `class` will be less likely to be chosen instead.

Here is an example where `predict.lda_schafer(model, newdata, type = "prob")` predicts a higher posterior probability for one class but `predict.lda_schafer(model, newdata, type = "class")` predicts the other:

```R
library(sparsediscrim)

set.seed(1)
x <- c(rnorm(30), rnorm(30) + 1)
y <- factor(c(rep("F", 30), rep("T", 30)), levels = c("F", "T"))
df <- data.frame(y = y, x = x)

mdl <- lda_schafer(y ~ x, df, prior = c(0.01, 0.99))
testx <- data.frame(x = 0)

predict(mdl, testx, "prob")  # Pr(F) < Pr(T)
predict(mdl, testx, "class")  # "F"
predict(mdl, testx, "score")  # score(F) < score(T)
```

In fact, according to equation (4.8) - (4.10) in [^1], I believe the correct score should be $\frac{1}{2}(x - \mu_k)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x - \mu_k) - \log(\pi_k)$ if the decision is based on lowest score. But in accordance with [^1], I think it will be more intuitive to use its negative $-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mu_k)^\top\Sigma^{-1}(x - \mu_k) + \log(\pi_k)$ and make decision based on highest score, so that the difference between the scores for two classes will be the same as the log of the posterior probability ratio between the two classes.

As a confirmation, continue to run:

```R
pr <- predict(mdl, testx, "prob")
sc <- predict(mdl, testx, "score")

print(paste("Log posterior ratio:", log(pr[["F", 1]] / pr[["T", 1]])))   # -3.72
print(paste("Difference between scores:", sc[[1, "F"]] - sc[[1, "T"]]))  # -6.34

# Correction
for (curr in names(sc)) {
    p <- mdl$est[[curr]]$prior
    sc[, curr] <- -0.5 * (sc[, curr] - log(p)) + log(p)
}
print(paste("Difference between new scores:", sc[[1, "F"]] - sc[[1, "T"]]))  # -3.72
```

Thanks for reading!

[^1]: Hastie, T., Tibshirani, R., & Friedman, J. H. (2009). *The elements of statistical learning: data mining, inference, and prediction* (Vol. 2, pp. 1-758). New York: springer.

title: Package Improvements Not Listed
description:
I was looking at the old package's code by John Ramey and noticed that it didn't check whether or not the variables names were the same in the test data set and inside the fittted model object. Test data set could be a whole table but trained model might have been fitted on a small subset of selected features. However, I notice that your version seems to elegantly take care of that using `process_newdata`. Is there a list somewhere of such improvements versus John's abandoned package?

For those readers of this issue using the John's package directly, a good way to subset your test data is:

```r
measurementsTest <- measurementsTest[, names(model[["var_pool"]])] # model is a trained DLDA object.
```

P.S. Predict functions from the popular e1071 also have the issue of not matching feature names to the trained model for robustness.
